content.title: About
content.content: Adobo is a traditional Filipino dish consisting of meat (usually chicken or pork) simmered in a sauce made from soy sauce, vinegar, garlic, onion and spices. The “Adobo with noodles” version adds boiled egg or wheat noodles to the classic sauce, making the meal heartier and convenient for quick service.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Adobo is considered the national dish of the Philippines and has many regional variations.
The word “adobo” comes from the Spanish “adobar” – “to marinate,” reflecting colonial influence.
The combination of vinegar and soy sauce allows the dish to be stored without refrigeration for a limited time.
Noodles are often cooked al dente before being mixed in, preserving texture during the final simmer.
Some versions incorporate coconut milk, giving the sauce a creamy note.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: The meat in adobo provides a high‑quality source of complete protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Source of vitamin B6
items.content: Vitamin B6 supports amino‑acid metabolism and nervous‑system function.

items.title: Probiotic‑like properties
items.content: The acidic environment created by soy sauce and vinegar can promote beneficial gut bacteria.

items.title: Energy‑providing carbs
items.content: Noodles add complex carbohydrates that deliver sustained energy and satiety.

items.title: Antioxidant compounds
items.content: Garlic and onion contain allicin and quercetin, which have antioxidant effects.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Soy sauce and the marinade can be very salty, which may be unsuitable for people with hypertension.

items.title: Soy allergy
items.content: Individuals allergic to soy should avoid this dish.

items.title: Acidity
items.content: Vinegar increases the dish’s acidity and may irritate the stomach of those with gastritis.

items.title: Fat content
items.content: Using pork can raise the amount of saturated fat.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve Adobo with noodles hot, garnished with fresh herbs such as cilantro or parsley. It can be eaten with a fork or chopsticks. Add a squeeze of lime or a dash of chili for extra brightness.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Cool the dish to room temperature, then store it in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. Reheat on the stovetop or in a microwave, adding a splash of water to keep it moist.

content.title: About
content.content: The falafel sandwich is a nutritious vegetarian sandwich featuring a spiced chickpea patty placed between slices of bread or wrapped in a flatbread together with vegetables, sauces, and herbs.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Falafel originated in the Middle East and is a staple in Mediterranean cuisines.
The chickpea patty is rich in plant protein and often used as a meat alternative.
There are many serving styles: in pita, in a wrap, on a bun, or as a standalone burger.
Traditionally falafel is deep‑fried, but it can also be baked for a lighter version.
In some regions beans are used instead of chickpeas in the mixture.

items.title: Rich in plant protein
items.content: Chickpeas, the main ingredient, provide about 20 g of protein per 100 g, supporting muscle maintenance.

items.title: High in dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber aids digestion and promotes a feeling of fullness.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: Falafel contains folate, thiamine, and niacin, important for energy metabolism.

items.title: Contains iron and magnesium
items.content: These minerals support blood formation and muscle function.

items.title: Low in saturated fat
items.content: When baked, falafel remains a low‑saturated‑fat option.

items.title: Legume allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to chickpeas.

items.title: High calories when fried
items.content: Traditional deep‑fried falafel can be calorie‑dense; portion control is advised.

items.title: Oxalate content
items.content: Chickpeas contain oxalates, which in excess may contribute to kidney stone formation.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the falafel sandwich hot, adding fresh veggies (tomato, cucumber, lettuce), sauces (tahini, yogurt, hummus), and aromatic herbs. It can be eaten by hand or with a fork.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the assembled sandwich in a sealed container in the refrigerator for up to 2‑3 days. Falafel patties can be frozen for up to 3 months; reheat before serving in an oven or microwave.

content.title: About
content.content: Flaxseeds are the small, shiny brown or golden seeds of the flax plant (Linum usitatissimum), one of the oldest cultivated crops. They have a mild, nutty flavor and are used whole or ground in baking, cereals, smoothies, and other foods. The flax plant is also grown for its fibers, which are used to make linen.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Flax has been cultivated for thousands of years for both its seeds and its fibers.
Flaxseeds come in brown and golden varieties with similar nutrition.
When soaked in water, flaxseeds form a gel-like substance.
Whole flaxseeds often pass through the body undigested, so grinding them improves nutrient absorption.
Ground flaxseed mixed with water is sometimes used as an egg substitute in baking.

items.title: Rich in ALA omega-3
items.content: Flaxseeds are one of the richest plant sources of alpha-linolenic acid, an omega-3 fatty acid.

items.title: Provides dietary fiber
items.content: Flaxseeds contain both soluble and insoluble fiber, which support digestion and regularity.

items.title: Contains lignans
items.content: Lignans are plant compounds with antioxidant properties that are being studied.

items.title: Source of protein and minerals
items.content: Flaxseeds provide plant protein, magnesium, and thiamin.

items.title: Easy to add to foods
items.content: Ground flaxseed can be mixed into many everyday foods.

items.title: Need to be ground
items.content: Whole flaxseeds may pass through the digestive system without being absorbed, so ground flaxseed is generally preferred.

items.title: Fiber and fluids
items.content: Eating flaxseeds without enough water may cause digestive discomfort or constipation, so drink plenty of fluids.

items.title: Possible medication interactions
items.content: The fiber in flaxseed may slow the absorption of some medications, and flaxseed may affect blood sugar or blood clotting. People taking prescription drugs should consult a healthcare professional.

items.title: Allergic reactions
items.content: Flaxseed allergy is uncommon but can occur. Eat flaxseed in moderate amounts.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Ground flaxseed can be stirred into oatmeal, yogurt, smoothies, and batters or added to bread, muffins, and pancakes. Whole seeds can be sprinkled on salads or baked into crackers and bread. Start with small amounts and drink plenty of water.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store whole flaxseeds in an airtight container in a cool, dark place. Ground flaxseed goes rancid faster, so keep it in the refrigerator or freezer in an airtight container. Discard seeds that smell bitter or like paint.

green-peas-frozen-cooked-fat-added-ns-as.title: Green peas, frozen, cooked, fat added

content.title: About
content.content: Green peas are young pea pods harvested before full maturity. In this product the peas are blanched, frozen, and a small amount of vegetable fat is added to enhance flavor and texture. They are ready to eat after reheating and retain most of their nutrients.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Frozen cooked peas are a common ingredient in ready‑made meals and soups because they heat up quickly.
Adding a modest amount of fat improves the absorption of fat‑soluble vitamins such as vitamin K and vitamin E.
Peas are one of the oldest cultivated crops, grown by humans for over 7,000 years.
Rapid freezing after cooking preserves the bright green color of the peas.
As a legume, peas can fix nitrogen in the soil, contributing to soil fertility.

items.title: Rich in plant protein
items.content: Green peas provide about 5 g of protein per 100 g, making them a good protein source for vegetarians.

items.title: High in dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber supports digestive health and promotes a feeling of fullness.

items.title: Source of vitamin K
items.content: Vitamin K is essential for blood clotting and bone health.

items.title: Contains folate
items.content: Folate is needed for DNA synthesis and is especially important during periods of rapid growth.

items.title: Helps regulate blood sugar
items.content: The low glycemic index of peas helps stabilize glucose levels after meals.

items.title: Legume allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience an allergic reaction to peas.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Prepared products may contain added salt; people monitoring sodium intake should check the label.

items.title: Added fats
items.content: The fat added is typically vegetable (e.g., sunflower oil) and may not be suitable for certain dietary restrictions.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Heat the frozen peas in the microwave or on the stovetop, seasoning as desired. They can be served as a side dish, added to salads, pastas, stews, or used as a filling for pies.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the frozen peas at –18 °C or lower. Once thawed, consume within 2–3 days and store in an airtight container in the refrigerator.

grilled-cheese-sandwich-reduced-fat-chee.title: Grilled Cheese Sandwich, Reduced Fat Cheese, on White Bread

content.title: About
content.content: A grilled cheese sandwich is made with a slice of white bread and reduced‑fat cheese, then toasted until the bread is golden and the cheese melts. The reduced‑fat cheese retains the creamy flavor of regular cheese while containing less fat.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Reduced‑fat cheese is produced from the same milk as regular cheese, but part of the fat is removed during processing.
White bread provides a neutral base that lets the cheese flavor shine.
Grilled cheese sandwiches became a staple in the United States in the mid‑20th century as a quick, inexpensive meal.
Toasting creates a crisp crust that traps heat, ensuring the cheese melts evenly.
The sandwich can be cooked in a toaster, on a skillet, or on a grill, each method giving a slightly different taste and texture.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Reduced‑fat cheese contains significantly less saturated fat, making the sandwich more suitable for low‑fat diets.

items.title: Source of protein
items.content: Cheese provides high‑quality dairy protein essential for muscle maintenance.

items.title: Calcium
items.content: Cheese is a good source of calcium, important for bone and teeth health.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Dairy products supply riboflavin (B2) and cobalamin (B12), supporting energy metabolism.

items.title: Moderate glycemic impact
items.content: White bread has a moderate glycemic index, and the protein from cheese helps slow blood‑sugar spikes.

items.title: Lactose intolerance
items.content: People with lactose intolerance may experience discomfort from dairy products, including reduced‑fat cheese.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Reduced‑fat cheese often contains added salt for flavor; those monitoring sodium intake should watch portion size.

items.title: Milk allergy
items.content: Allergy to milk proteins (casein) can cause reactions in sensitive individuals.

items.title: Bread quality
items.content: White bread is low in fiber; frequent consumption should be balanced with whole‑grain options.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the sandwich hot, cut diagonally. It can be paired with fresh vegetables (tomato slices, lettuce) or a light spread. For a lighter version, use whole‑grain bread.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Grilled cheese is best enjoyed immediately. If you need to store it, let it cool to room temperature, then place in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 24 hours. Bread may become soggy, so reheat with a little butter or olive oil to restore crispness.

grits-instant-made-with-water-fat-added.title: Grits, instant, made with water, fat added

content.title: About
content.content: Grits are finely ground corn kernels designed for quick preparation. This instant version is meant to be cooked with water and a small amount of added fat, making the dish richer and more flavorful. Grits are commonly used as a side dish or a breakfast base.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Grits originated in the Southern United States as a staple of low‑cost cooking.
Instant grits cook in 5‑7 minutes, ideal for busy schedules.
Corn, the base of grits, is rich in carotenoids that give it a yellow hue.
Traditional grits are often served with cheese, butter, or milk.
Grits can be turned into sweet dishes with fruit, honey, or maple syrup.

items.title: Source of complex carbohydrates
items.content: Grits provide slowly digestible energy, helping to maintain stable blood sugar levels.

items.title: Contains dietary fiber
items.content: Corn fiber supports healthy digestion and promotes satiety.

items.title: Rich in B‑vitamins
items.content: Grits contain thiamine, niacin, and folate, which are important for metabolism.

items.title: Provides iron
items.content: Iron in grits helps maintain normal hemoglobin levels.

items.title: Contains magnesium
items.content: Magnesium contributes to muscle and nerve function.

items.title: Corn allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to corn products.

items.title: High sodium in some mixes
items.content: Certain instant grits contain added salt; people with hypertension should monitor portion size.

items.title: Fat content
items.content: Added fat increases caloric density; those watching weight should account for it in their diet.

content.title: How to Prepare
content.content: Bring water to a boil, add the grits and a small amount of fat (butter, cream, or oil). Stir well and simmer for 5‑7 minutes until tender. Season with salt, spices, cheese, or fresh herbs as desired.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the dry instant grits in a cool, dry place, keeping the package tightly sealed. After opening, transfer to an airtight container. Shelf life is indicated on the packaging.

okra-frozen-cooked-no-added-fat.title: Okra, frozen, cooked, no added fat

content.title: About
content.content: Okra (Abelmoschus esculentus) is an edible pod widely used in African, Asian, and American cuisines. The frozen version is quickly steamed and packaged without added fat, preserving most nutrients and its characteristic tender flavor.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Okra is also known as "lady's finger", "gumbo" and "bush okra".
Its mucilaginous content helps regulate blood sugar levels.
In the United States okra is a key ingredient in gumbo, while in India it is common in curries.
Freezing retains up to 90 % of vitamin C, which is often lost in fresh pods during storage.
Okra is rich in antioxidants such as quercetin and kaempferol.

items.title: High in dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber supports healthy digestion and promotes satiety.

items.title: Low calorie content
items.content: A 100 g serving provides about 20 kcal, making it an excellent choice for weight‑management diets.

items.title: Contains vitamin C and vitamin K
items.content: Vitamin C boosts immunity, while vitamin K is essential for blood clotting.

items.title: Source of minerals
items.content: Okra provides magnesium, potassium and iron, important for muscle and nerve function.

items.title: Supports blood‑sugar control
items.content: The mucilage slows glucose absorption, helping to stabilize glycemia.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to okra.

items.title: Oxalate content
items.content: Okra contains oxalates, which can contribute to kidney stone formation in susceptible people.

items.title: Texture issues if overcooked
items.content: Overheating can make the pods overly soft and slimy, which may be undesirable for some.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Thaw the pods in the refrigerator or under running water, then quickly sauté, add to soups, stews, salads, or use as a side dish. It can also be blended into smoothies for extra nutrition.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the frozen okra in its original packaging at –18 °C. After thawing, use within 2–3 days and store in an airtight container in the refrigerator.

content.title: About
content.content: Tahini is a paste made from ground toasted sesame seeds, widely used in Middle Eastern, Mediterranean and Asian cuisines. It has a creamy texture, nutty aroma and a slightly bitter taste. Tahini serves as the base for hummus, baba ganoush, sauces, desserts and baked goods.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Tahini is made from fully toasted sesame seeds, which gives it its distinctive flavor.
In Israel, tahini is considered a national staple and appears in almost every dish.
Sesame is one of the oldest cultivated plants, grown for more than 5,000 years.
Tahini is often used in vegan recipes as an egg or dairy substitute.
In some countries tahini is sold as a runny paste, while in others it is thick, almost chocolate‑like.

items.title: Rich in healthy fats
items.content: Tahini contains monounsaturated and polyunsaturated fatty acids that support heart health.

items.title: Source of calcium
items.content: Sesame is one of the richest plant sources of calcium, essential for bones and teeth.

items.title: Contains iron
items.content: Tahini helps replenish iron stores, especially important in vegetarian diets.

items.title: High in magnesium
items.content: Magnesium in tahini supports muscle and nerve function.

items.title: Contains antioxidants
items.content: Sesamol and sesamin are antioxidants that protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Sesame allergy
items.content: Sesame is a major allergen; reactions can be severe.

items.title: High calorie density
items.content: Tahini is calorie‑dense, so portion sizes should be moderated.

items.title: Oxalate content
items.content: Sesame contains oxalates, which may contribute to kidney stone formation in susceptible individuals.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Use tahini as the base for sauces (hummus, tahini sauce), blend into smoothies, desserts, baked goods, salad dressings and marinades. It can be thinned with water, lemon juice and spices to create a smooth sauce.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store tahini in a tightly sealed jar in a cool, dark place. For longer shelf life keep it in the refrigerator, where it stays fresh for up to 6 months. Discard if it develops a rancid smell or taste.

content.title: About
content.content: Tomatoes are the edible fruits of the tomato plant (Solanum lycopersicum) cultivated worldwide. Fresh tomatoes are juicy with a mildly sweet‑tart flavor, while cooking softens them and retains most nutrients.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Botanically tomatoes are berries, though culinarily they are treated as vegetables.
There are over 10,000 tomato varieties differing in color, shape, and taste.
Lycopene gives tomatoes their red color and is a powerful antioxidant.
Tomatoes were first domesticated in South America more than 7,000 years ago.
They are a major source of the antioxidant lycopene.

items.title: Rich in vitamin C
items.content: Vitamin C supports the immune system and collagen synthesis.

items.title: Contains lycopene
items.content: Lycopene has antioxidant properties and may reduce the risk of certain cancers.

items.title: Low in calories
items.content: Tomatoes are suitable for weight‑management diets due to their low calorie density.

items.title: Source of potassium
items.content: Potassium helps regulate blood pressure and supports heart function.

items.title: Provides dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber aids digestion and promotes satiety.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to tomatoes.

items.title: Acidity
items.content: High acidity can aggravate gastritis or heartburn in sensitive people.

items.title: Pesticide residues
items.content: Unwashed tomatoes may contain pesticide residues; rinse thoroughly before use.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Fresh tomatoes are enjoyed in salads, sandwiches, salsas, and juices. Cooked tomatoes are used in soups, stews, sauces, and casseroles. They can also be roasted, grilled, or steamed.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store fresh tomatoes at room temperature away from direct light for up to 5‑7 days. Cooked tomatoes should be kept in a sealed container in the refrigerator for 3‑4 days. Discard any that become soft, moldy, or develop an off‑odor.

content.title: About
content.content: Greek yogurt made from nonfat milk is a thick, creamy product with high protein and low fat. It is produced by double‑straining, which removes much of the whey and creates a denser texture compared with regular yogurt.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Greek yogurt contains two to three times more protein than regular yogurt.
Nonfat milk retains most nutrients while removing almost all fat.
Traditionally, Greek yogurt is set in a temperature‑controlled environment and then strained through cheesecloth or a special filter.
Its thick consistency makes it a popular substitute for sour cream or mayonnaise in recipes.
Greek yogurt surged in popularity in the United States in the early 2000s as a high‑protein snack.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: One cup (≈200 g) provides about 20 g of high‑quality protein, supporting muscle growth and repair.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Made from nonfat milk, the product is virtually fat‑free, suitable for calorie‑restricted diets.

items.title: Source of probiotics
items.content: Live cultures promote gut health and may strengthen the immune system.

items.title: Calcium and vitamin D
items.content: Greek yogurt supplies a substantial portion of the daily calcium requirement, important for bone health.

items.title: Low glycemic index
items.content: The high protein and low sugar content result in a modest impact on blood glucose levels.

items.title: Lactose intolerance
items.content: Although much of the lactose is removed during straining, a small amount remains.

items.title: Milk protein allergy
items.content: Casein and whey proteins can trigger allergic reactions in sensitive individuals.

items.title: Added sugars
items.content: Some brands sweeten the product; choose an unsweetened version if you watch sugar intake.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Certain varieties may contain added salt, which should be considered on low‑sodium diets.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Enjoy it plain as a snack, blend into smoothies, use in sauces, dips, desserts, or as a base for dressings. Its thick texture pairs well with berries, nuts, honey, or whole‑grain cereals.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the yogurt refrigerated at 1‑4 °C. Once opened, consume within 5‑7 days and do not leave at room temperature for more than 2 hours.
